1f5ef773-6fe6-4b0b-8631-3c457a698dfd.recap: The host covers a rescue of Volksbank Bravo, a small German cooperative bank (€6.5bn in assets) receiving up to €723m in support -- €473m in guarantees plus a roughly €250m equity stake -- from the cooperative sector's mutual protection system after identifying ~€608m in potential value losses, 96% from non-core investments in corporate credit, equity, and real estate rather than traditional mortgage or SME lending. A second cooperative bank, Volksbank Cleveland, has also sought help after an internal loan review and after firing its former CEO for governance failures. Transfers into the sector's shared 'bad bank' (BAG) hit €1.2bn last year, a 20-year high, over 5x the prior year, and 2026 rescue contributions are expected to more than double versus 2025. The host frames this as the end product of a decade of yield-reaching by institutions (German cooperatives, pension funds, insurers, private credit managers) forced out of low-yielding safe assets into private credit, mezzanine debt, and property, all of which looked fine while valuations rose. He ties this to CCC-rated bond spreads near 1,100bp (distressed territory, per guest Peter Boockvar), record private credit default rates (Fitch) driven by distressed maturity extensions ('extend and pretend'), and a collapse in BDC fundraising (from $11bn to $2bn). None of this signals a systemic deposit run or interbank freeze -- the German mutual system is functioning as designed -- but the host argues it shows credit risk being repriced globally across very different accounting regimes simultaneously.

34bce5a2-0de0-4988-af0d-0d33833565ee.recap: Kevin Coldiron interviews FT journalist Robin Wigglesworth about his new book on the history of bonds. Most of the conversation traces how bond market 'technology' built state power: Venice's 12th-century forced war loan (prestiti) became the first tradable bond and later consolidated into a single homogeneous issue (monte), Britain's consolidated annuities became arguably the first reserve asset because parliamentary checks on the crown made repayment credible, and the post-WWII Eurodollar glut (dollars pooling offshore, partly from Soviet-bloc banks) seeded the stateless Eurobond market that rebuilt London as a financial center. A long section covers Michael Milken, who read economist Braddock Hickman's finding that diversified low-rated bonds outperform after defaults, then built an original-issue junk bond market (rather than just trading fallen angels) at Drexel Burnham Lambert, birthing the modern leveraged finance and private credit industry -- though later vintages of junk defaulted more as quality diluted. Wigglesworth argues fixed-income ETFs have unexpectedly improved bond market liquidity rather than harming it, interacting with electronification and portfolio trading, and flags tokenization (already growing in repo) as an underappreciated coming shift. The interview closes on current events: Treasury Secretary Bessent's expanded liquidity buybacks, which Wigglesworth dismisses as largely symbolic ('peeing on a forest fire') relative to total issuance, but acknowledges are aimed at dampening volatility to protect hedge funds' heavily levered Treasury basis trade -- with the real fix being Fed chair Kevin Warsh signaling openness to rate hikes to rein in above-target inflation and rising term premium.
terms: Eurodollar -- offshore US dollar deposits/bonds held outside the US banking system
basis trade -- levered arbitrage going long Treasury cash bonds and short Treasury futures to capture the price difference
term premium -- extra yield investors demand for holding longer-dated bonds over expected short-rate path
fallen angel -- a bond originally issued investment-grade that is later downgraded to junk

36a100b4-b21e-11f1-83b5-7f87dc57cd53.recap: Joseph Wang (ex-NY Fed trader) and host Jack review the FOMC meeting under Chair Kevin Warsh, who hiked rates for the first time in his tenure -- exactly as Wang predicted after parsing Warsh's Jackson Hole language about financial conditions not being restrictive and the 'speed' of returning to target. The vote was unanimous, and Warsh reframed the hike as 'removing a dose of accommodation,' implying policy is still accommodative and more hikes (Wang expects at least two) are coming. The dot plot showed one more hike this year but, more notably, raised the 2028 median rate 50bp (3.4% to 3.9%), signaling a higher-for-longer neutral rate. Warsh cited strong growth, low unemployment, sticky inflation, and geopolitical/energy shocks (Strait of Hormuz disruption pushing oil above $100) as reasons the Fed can no longer look through supply shocks after years of repeated ones. On plumbing: Wang notes repo/SOFR volumes are unusually low because basis traders have stepped back, reducing financing demand and possibly contributing to long-end Treasury weakness; he also expects the Fed to shift balance-sheet composition toward bills, mirroring Treasury's own shift in issuance. They also discuss Treasury's buyback program, upsized to $6bn per operation but under-executed at ~$4.5-5.1bn, disappointing markets hoping for a bigger yield-suppression 'bazooka.' A second segment covers a booming refining-stock trade (Marathon Petroleum, Valero) driven by wide crack spreads from the Hormuz-related supply shock, and a debate on whether AI capex financing is more sensitive to short-end (SOFR, neoclouds/private credit) versus long-end rates.

42f42640-cfc8-4f09-ad32-6c9850a83e56.recap: Jeffrey Gundlach of DoubleLine discusses stretched equity valuations (Shiller CAPE ~42) alongside rising Treasury yields, and pivots to credit market cracks. He notes triple-C bank loans and AI-related high-yield/loan spreads have widened meaningfully (junk bonds ~50bp, bank loans ~130bp off tights) while non-AI credit remains firm, citing SpaceX and Oracle bond issuance trading well wide of their assigned ratings. He argues rating agencies are being arbitraged, especially in private credit, where firms can shop among ~7-8 agencies for favorable ratings that flatter insurer capital treatment and leverage. He describes an incestuous chain: private equity owns private credit, which is bought by affiliated insurance/reinsurance companies (often offshore, under-reserved, and lightly regulated at the state level), calling private credit "the fuse" and insurance "the bomb." He draws a 2006/CDO-ratings analogy, recommends buying annuities/life insurance only from mutual companies, and details his own portfolio shift to just 10% gold, dry powder in short-duration/high-quality funds, and zero AI exposure. On rates, he explains a model regressing the 7-year moving average of US nominal GDP against the German 10-year yield (R²=0.93) to argue the US 10-year is ~20bp rich to fair value. He also flags Treasury's "Operation Twist"-style signaling via Bessent, expects the Fed's two-year note dynamics to force a possible 25bp hike, and forecasts CPI printing above 4% into next year on oil (above $100/barrel) and diesel price spikes.

marketmatters.podbean.com/6febfd17-4f61-.recap: Brian LaRocca (JPMorgan Vita Portfolio Solutions) interviews Ben Kenney, newly head of credit sales after running rate sales, on how rates-market discipline is bleeding into credit. Kenney argues credit now has near-continuous price discovery: H1 2026 IG bond turnover hit an 18-year high, HY daily turnover (still under 1%) is the highest since 2020, and roughly 98.7% of IG CUSIPs and over 97% of HY CUSIPs trade at least once weekly, up from 95% a year ago. He sees credit electronification at the 'third or fourth inning,' behind FX and rates, with portfolio trading maturing faster in credit than it ever did in rates. On macro, he flags unusual policy uncertainty (new Fed chair Kevin Warsh scrapping forward guidance/dot plots, Treasury Secretary Bessent actively pushing yields lower, large deficits) and says he'd rather express the view via FX than duration or front-end rates given the noise, though fiscal steepening pressure remains real. On the ~$300bn data-center-driven IG issuance wave (IG issuance +50% YoY), he attributes summer spread widening partly to equity-market deleveraging noise rather than pure credit indigestion, expects continued issuance-driven volatility over the next 6-9 months, and says concentration limits aren't binding yet but are a growing medium-term risk. On private credit, the 'SAS apocalypse' narrative has repriced but isn't resolved — gates remain up, redemptions are restricted, and a 2028-29 refinancing wall looms though it's viewed as manageable rather than systemic. He also flags China capital formation and AI funding as an underappreciated risk. Low June/July default rates coexist with a slowly rising share of HY trading at distressed levels.

BDC -- Business development company, a vehicle used to hold private credit loans
TBAC -- Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee, which advises the U.S. Treasury on debt issuance
ABL -- Asset-based lending, financing secured against a borrower's collateral pool
LevFin -- Leveraged finance, the business of underwriting and trading sub-investment-grade loans and bonds
